stem: A bookshop designs a relational database with a Customer table, a Book table and an Order table. In the Customer table, what does a single row represent?

choices.text: One relationship that links the Customer table to the Order table through a matching value.
One instance of the customer entity, holding all of the recorded data for a single customer.
One data type that the database allows in the table, such as text, integer or date values.
One attribute that is recorded for every customer, such as the email address of each person.

stem: A Customer table has a MiddleName column. Many customers have no middle name, or the company does not know it. How should the column be defined so these customers can still be stored?

choices.text: Define the column as NOT NULL so the database stores an empty text string whenever no value is supplied.
Define the column as the primary key so the database fills in a unique value for each row that has none.
Define the column as nullable so rows can be saved with no value, which the database records as NULL.
Define the column as a foreign key so the missing value is looked up from a related table automatically.

stem: A sales spreadsheet stores "Jane Smith, 42 Oak St Seattle" in one cell and the price "9.99 USD" as text. The team moves it into a relational table with a separate column for each attribute. Which TWO benefits does this give? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Each value can be constrained to a suitable data type, such as decimal for prices and integer for quantities.
The table no longer needs a primary key, because every column now holds just one separate piece of data.
The database stops needing data types at all, because one value per column is already clear to every reader.
Queries can easily filter on a single attribute, such as finding only the customers who live in Seattle.
The table can store a different set of columns for each row, so every customer keeps only the fields it uses.

stem: An Employee table has an EmployeeID column. Every employee gets a different EmployeeID, and the database must reject any row that repeats an existing ID or leaves it empty. What is EmployeeID?

choices.text: An index, because it holds a sorted copy of the column with pointers back to the table rows.
A foreign key, because it stores a value that refers to a row in another table of the database.
A primary key, because it uniquely identifies each row and can't hold duplicate or NULL values.
A view, because it presents a virtual table built from the results of a SELECT query on the data.

stem: An Order table must record which customer placed each order, and customer details such as the address are stored only in a Customer table whose primary key is ID. What should the Order table contain?

choices.text: A second primary key that combines the order number with the customer's name, so both stay unique together.
A copy of the customer's name and address columns in every order row, so each order can be read on its own.
A view named Customer inside the Order table that lists the customer's details for each order number.
A CustomerID column defined as a foreign key that holds the ID of the related row in the Customer table.

stem: In an OrderLine table, OrderNo alone repeats for each item on an order and ItemNo alone repeats across orders, but each OrderNo and ItemNo pair occurs only once. How can each line be uniquely identified?

choices.text: Define a composite primary key on OrderNo and ItemNo, because their combination is unique for every line.
Define an index on OrderNo only, because a sorted index makes every value of the column unique by itself.
Define two separate primary keys, one on OrderNo and one on ItemNo, so each column is checked on its own.
Define a foreign key from ItemNo to OrderNo, because linking the two columns makes every line distinct.

stem: An app tries to insert an order with CustomerID 950, but no customer with ID 950 exists. The database rejects the insert. Which relational feature caused this?

choices.text: Normalization, which blocks any row that would duplicate data already held in a different table of the database.
Referential integrity from a foreign key, which requires the value to match an existing primary key row.
An index on the CustomerID column, which refuses values that are not already present in its sorted copy of data.
A NOT NULL constraint on the CustomerID column, which requires that every new order supplies a customer value.

stem: A company tracks sales in one spreadsheet where the customer's address is repeated on every sale. When a customer moves, staff must edit dozens of rows and sometimes miss some. How does a normalized relational design fix this?

choices.text: It adds an index on the address column so every repeated copy of the address can be found and edited together.
It creates a view over the spreadsheet so the address shown in each row can be edited in one place at once.
It keeps all data in one wide table but makes the address column NOT NULL so no row can be missed by staff.
It stores the address once in a Customer table, and orders reference that row, so a move changes a single row.

stem: A junior developer reads that a schema should be normalized. Which TWO are practical rules of normalization? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Use foreign key columns to link related entities, such as an order to the customer that placed it.
Combine related attributes, such as name and address, into one column so each row stays shorter.
Keep a copy of each customer's details on every order so that each order row can be read on its own.
Store every entity in one shared table so that no join is ever needed to read the related data.
Separate each entity, such as customers and products, into its own table in the database schema.

stem: A developer writes a script with the statements CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE and DROP TABLE. To which group of SQL statements do these belong?

choices.text: Transaction control statements, which commit or roll back a group of changes as one unit of database work.
Data Definition Language (DDL), which creates, modifies and removes tables and other database objects.
Data Manipulation Language (DML), which reads rows from tables and adds, changes or removes those rows.
Data Control Language (DCL), which grants, denies or revokes permissions on objects for users and groups.

stem: A database administrator must let a reporting user named user1 read and add rows in the Product table without changing any table design. Which statement fits?

choices.text: `ALTER TABLE Product ADD user1 VARCHAR(20);`, adding the user to the table so it can read and insert rows.
`INSERT INTO Product (user1) VALUES ('SELECT');`, storing the user's allowed actions as a row in the table.
`GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON Product TO user1;`, giving the user permission to read and add rows in the table.
`CREATE VIEW user1 AS SELECT * FROM Product;`, creating a view named after the user that it can edit freely.

stem: Last month a DBA granted user2 permission to update the Price table. That access is no longer needed, and the DBA wants simply to remove the earlier grant. Which DCL statement does this?

choices.text: `DROP`, which removes a permission from the database permanently so it can't be granted to any user again later.
`DENY`, which removes a permission that was given earlier and returns the user to having no explicit permission.
`REVOKE`, which removes a permission that was previously granted so the user no longer has it on that table.
`DELETE`, which removes the stored permission row for the user from the table the permission was granted on.

stem: Which TWO statements belong to Data Manipulation Language (DML), the group that works with the rows stored in tables? (Select TWO)

choices.text: `UPDATE`, which modifies the data in rows that already exist in a table, usually matched by a WHERE clause.
`GRANT`, which gives a user or group the permission to perform specific actions on a database object.
`CREATE`, which adds a new object to the database, such as a table, a view or a stored procedure.
`ALTER`, which modifies the structure of an existing table, for example by adding a new column to the table.
`INSERT`, which adds new rows to a table, with a list of values for the columns named in the statement.

stem: A developer meant to change the address of customer 1 and ran `UPDATE Customer SET Address = '123 High St.';`. Now every customer has that address. What caused this?

choices.text: The Address column was defined as NOT NULL, so the database copied the new value into every row of the table.
The statement used UPDATE instead of ALTER, and only ALTER can change the value of a single row in a table.
The Customer table had no index on the Address column, so the change was applied to the whole table instead.
The statement had no WHERE clause, so UPDATE applied the new value to every row in the Customer table.

stem: A Promotions table holds last year's offers. The team wants to remove all of its rows but keep the table, with its columns and keys, ready for new offers. Which statement fits?

choices.text: `REVOKE SELECT ON Promotions;`, which hides every existing row so that only newly inserted rows are visible.
`DELETE FROM Promotions;`, which removes every row of data while the table itself stays in the database.
`DROP TABLE Promotions;`, which empties the table's rows while keeping the column definitions for reuse.
`ALTER TABLE Promotions;`, which resets the table to its original empty state with the same set of columns.

stem: An existing Product table needs a new Weight column. The table already holds thousands of rows that must be kept. Which type of statement should the developer run?

choices.text: A `CREATE TABLE` statement, a DDL statement that adds the column by defining the Product table a second time.
An `ALTER TABLE` statement, a DDL statement that modifies the structure of the existing table to add the column.
An `INSERT` statement, a DML statement that adds the Weight column by inserting a row that holds its name.
An `UPDATE` statement, a DML statement that adds the new column to every existing row along with a value.

stem: A report runs `SELECT FirstName, LastName FROM Customer WHERE City = 'Seattle';`. Users complain the names come back in a different order on different days. What should be added?

choices.text: A `GROUP BY LastName` clause, which keeps rows in the order they were first inserted into the Customer table.
An index on the City column, which makes the database always return rows sorted by the indexed column value.
A primary key on the LastName column, which forces the table to store and return rows sorted by last name.
An `ORDER BY LastName` clause, which sorts the returned rows by the LastName column every time it runs.

stem: An Order table has a CustomerID foreign key and a Customer table holds addresses under the primary key ID. A query must list each order number with its customer's city. What should the query use?

choices.text: A `UNION` that stacks the rows of the Order table on top of the Customer table, matched by the column order.
An `ALTER TABLE` that adds a City column to Order, so the query can read the city from one table only.
A `JOIN` that matches Order.CustomerID with Customer.ID, so each order row is combined with its customer row.
A `GRANT` that lets the Order table read the Customer table, so the city appears in the order rows directly.

stem: A marketing list must show every customer, including customers who have never placed an order. Orders that exist should appear beside each customer. Which join gives this result?

choices.text: A left outer join from Customer to Order, which keeps every customer and shows NULL where no order matches.
An inner join from Order to Customer, which returns every order and adds the customers who have no orders.
An inner join from Customer to Order, which returns all customers and fills in orders where they exist.
A cross join between Customer and Order, which pairs each customer only with the orders that customer placed.

stem: Analysts often need order numbers with each customer's name and delivery address, which requires joining the Order and Customer tables. The DBA wants to give them one object they can query like a table. What should the DBA create?

choices.text: An index on the Order and Customer tables, which stores the joined columns so analysts can query the index.
A view defined by a SELECT that joins Order and Customer, which analysts can query and filter like a table.
A foreign key between Order and Customer, which lets analysts read both tables as one combined table.
A new table that copies the joined order and customer data, refreshed by hand whenever an analyst asks.

stem: Several applications rename products by running the same UPDATE logic with a product ID and a new name. The team wants that logic kept inside the database and run on command with parameters. Which object fits?

choices.text: A view, which stores a SELECT query and lets applications pass a product ID to update the matching row.
An index, which keeps a sorted copy of the Name column so applications can change product names faster.
A stored procedure, which holds SQL statements with parameters that applications run on command with EXEC.
A foreign key, which links each product row to its new name stored in a separate table of product names.

stem: A Product table has millions of rows, and a search page runs `SELECT * FROM Product WHERE Name = @name;` many times a minute. Each query scans the whole table and is slow. What should be added?

choices.text: An index on the Name column, so the database can find matching rows without reading every row.
A foreign key on the Name column, so the database links each name to the matching product row.
A view on the Product table that selects the Name column, so the search page reads fewer rows.
A stored procedure that runs the SELECT, so the database caches the full Product table in memory.

stem: To speed up reports, a developer added indexes on almost every column of a busy Orders table. Reports are faster, but inserting and updating orders is now slower. Which TWO explain this? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Indexes lock the table as read-only until the database rebuilds them each night, so changes wait in a queue.
Indexes make the foreign keys on the table check every row of the related tables before each new insert.
Indexes turn the Orders table into a view, so every insert must first run the view's SELECT statement again.
Each index stores its own sorted copy of column data, so many indexes consume extra storage space as well.
Each index must be maintained whenever rows are inserted, updated or deleted, which adds work to every change.

stem: A team lead lists facts about primary keys in SQL Server and Azure SQL Database for new hires. Which TWO statements are correct? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The columns of a primary key can't contain NULL, because every row must be identifiable by its key value.
A primary key is required on every table, and the database refuses to create a table that is defined without one.
A table can have several primary key constraints, one for each column that holds unique values in the table.
Primary key values may repeat across rows as long as at least one other column in the row is different.
The database enforces uniqueness of a primary key by automatically creating a unique index on its columns.

stem: Which statement correctly describes the difference between a view and an index in a relational database?

choices.text: A view stores a full copy of a table's rows for faster reads; an index is a saved query that combines tables.
A view is a virtual table based on a SELECT query; an index is a sorted copy of column data used to find rows fast.
A view runs parameterized SQL logic on command; an index links rows in one table to rows in another table.
A view grants permissions to users on selected rows; an index removes rows that are no longer needed by queries.

stem: A team uses Azure SQL Database and also an Azure Database for PostgreSQL server. A new developer asks why the procedural code for each looks slightly different. Which explanation is correct?

choices.text: Only Azure SQL Database supports SQL; PostgreSQL uses its own query language that is unrelated to the SQL standard.
Both systems use PL/SQL exactly, and the differences come only from the editor tools the developers have chosen.
Each system uses its own SQL dialect; Azure SQL Database uses Transact-SQL, and PostgreSQL uses PL/pgSQL.
Azure SQL Database uses PL/pgSQL and PostgreSQL uses Transact-SQL, so each team must learn the other's dialect.

stem: A developer writes `CREATE TABLE Product (ID INT PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL, Price DECIMAL NULL);`. Which statement about the new table is correct?

choices.text: Name can hold whole numbers only, because VARCHAR stores integer values of up to twenty digits in length.
ID may repeat across rows, because a PRIMARY KEY only sorts the rows and does not enforce any uniqueness.
Price must always have a value, because DECIMAL columns are mandatory in every row of a relational table.
ID uniquely identifies each row, Name is a mandatory text column, and Price may be left empty as NULL.

stem: A startup is building a new cloud-native web application that needs one relational database. The team wants the latest stable SQL Server features and no responsibility for operating systems, patching or backups. Which Azure service fits best?

choices.text: Azure SQL Database as a single database, with its own dedicated resources managed through a logical server.
SQL Server on an Azure virtual machine, installed from a SQL Server image in the Azure Marketplace.
Azure SQL Managed Instance, deployed into a dedicated subnet of the startup's own Azure virtual network.
Azure Database for MySQL flexible server, running the MySQL Community Edition engine that Azure manages.

stem: A software company sells a SaaS app and gives each of its 300 customers a separate Azure SQL Database. Most databases are idle most of the day, but each one has short, unpredictable peaks. The company wants to cut costs without starving any database at its peak. What should it use?

choices.text: The Business Critical service tier for every database, so that each one keeps a local read-only replica for peaks.
A larger SQL Server VM size, so that all databases run inside one instance whose memory and CPU can be resized.
One SQL Managed Instance, so that all 300 customers share a single database with a tenant ID column in each table.
An elastic pool, so that the databases share a set amount of compute and storage purchased for the whole group.

stem: Which statement correctly describes an Azure SQL Database elastic pool?

choices.text: A collection of SQL Managed Instances in one subnet that share one set of logins, jobs and linked servers.
A set of compute and storage resources shared by several databases on one logical server, billed for the pool.
A cluster of SQL Server virtual machines that together host one very large database split across many nodes.
A group of database copies kept in several Azure regions so that the application can fail over during an outage.

stem: A company runs an on-premises SQL Server instance with 40 databases. The applications use SQL Server Agent jobs, cross-database queries and linked servers. It wants a managed PaaS service and as few application changes as possible. Which service should it choose?

choices.text: Azure SQL Database in an elastic pool, so that all 40 databases share resources and keep running their Agent jobs.
SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines, which provides full SQL Server compatibility and access to the operating system.
Azure SQL Managed Instance, which provides a SQL Server instance with near-100% compatibility as a managed service.
Azure SQL Database single databases, one per on-premises database, managed together through one logical server.

stem: A manufacturer's SQL Server database works with a vendor monitoring agent that must be installed on the same server as SQL Server and needs access to the operating system. It wants to move to Azure quickly without changing anything. Which option should it use?

choices.text: Azure SQL Managed Instance, because it has near-100% compatibility with SQL Server Enterprise Edition features.
Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server, because it lets you add extensions that run inside the database.
SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines, because it gives full control of the SQL Server engine and the operating system.
Azure SQL Database Hyperscale, because it separates compute and storage and scales to very large databases.

services: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines

stem: Which TWO Azure services for SQL Server workloads are platform as a service (PaaS) offerings? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Azure SQL Managed Instance, a fully managed instance with near-100% compatibility.
SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines, a VM image with SQL Server already installed.
Azure Dedicated Host, a physical server reserved for VMs that run the SQL Server engine.
Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets running SQL Server Express on several identical VMs.
Azure SQL Database, a fully managed database designed for new cloud applications.

services: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines

stem: A team moves a database from SQL Server on an Azure VM to Azure SQL Database. Which TWO tasks will Microsoft perform for the team after the move? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Deciding which indexes to create and rewriting slow queries that the application sends to the database.
Applying updates and patches to the database engine and to the operating system underneath it.
Creating database logins and users and granting them permissions on the tables of the database.
Choosing which application data to keep, which to delete and how sensitive each column of data is.
Taking automatic database backups that the team can use for a point-in-time restore when needed.

stem: A developer needs an Azure SQL Database for a test environment that is used for a few hours on some days and sits idle for long periods. She wants compute charges only while the database is in use. Which option fits best?

choices.text: The Hyperscale service tier with read-only geo-replicas, which turn off compute in the primary when idle.
An elastic pool with one database in it, which bills only for the minutes when the database runs queries.
The provisioned compute tier, which keeps a fixed amount of compute allocated and billed every hour of the day.
The serverless compute tier, which scales compute with demand and can pause the database when it is inactive.

stem: In Azure SQL Database, what is the role of the logical server (the SQL Database server) that you create along with your databases?

choices.text: A central administrative point for its databases, holding logins, firewall rules, auditing and failover groups.
A full SQL Server instance with its own SQL Server Agent, Database Mail and linked servers for its databases.
A virtual machine that you sign in to with Remote Desktop to install SQL Server updates for the databases.
A physical host reserved for your company so that no other Azure customer's databases run on the hardware.

stem: Which Azure SQL option gives a database administrator the experience most similar to running SQL Server in the company's own datacenter, including full control of the instance and the operating system?

choices.text: Azure SQL Managed Instance, deployed into the company's Azure virtual network.
Azure SQL Database in an elastic pool, managed through a single logical server.
Azure SQL Database serverless, which scales compute automatically with demand.
SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines, running on Windows Server or Linux VMs.

services: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines

stem: A team moved its SQL Server database to a single Azure VM and assumed the VM's availability SLA protected the database. During a SQL Server service crash, the VM stayed up but the database was offline. What explains this?

choices.text: The VM SLA applies only when the database is also registered in an Azure SQL Database elastic pool on the same logical server.
Microsoft restarts SQL Server automatically only on Linux VMs, so the team should have chosen a Linux image for the database.
The VM SLA covers the virtual machines, not the SQL Server processes on them, so database high availability is the team's job.
SQL Server on Azure VMs supports only the Express edition, which has no automatic restart of the database service after a crash.

services: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines

stem: An app that will move to Azure uses SQL Server CLR assemblies inside the database. The team prefers a PaaS service so that Microsoft handles patching. Which service supports this with the fewest changes?

choices.text: SQL Server on Azure VMs, because Microsoft patches the operating system and SQL Server for all VM images.
Azure SQL Managed Instance, because CLR modules are among the SQL Server features it supports as a PaaS service.
Azure SQL Database as a single database, because it runs the latest stable SQL Server Enterprise Edition engine.
Azure SQL Database in an elastic pool, because pooled databases can load assemblies from the shared resources.

stem: A bank needs its managed SQL Server databases to use private IP addresses inside its own Azure virtual network, with connectivity to on-premises over ExpressRoute, and it relies on instance-level features. Which service fits best?

choices.text: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines in a public subnet, with the operating system firewall left open to clients.
Azure Database for MySQL flexible server, which is based on the community edition and offers zone-redundant HA.
Azure SQL Managed Instance, which is deployed with a native virtual network implementation and private IP addresses.
Azure SQL Database single databases, reached from the internet through the logical server's firewall rules.

stem: Which TWO capabilities does SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines offer that Azure SQL Database does not? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Choosing when operating system and SQL Server updates are installed, and installing extra software on the host.
Built-in high availability of the database itself, covered by Microsoft without any extra configuration.
Online changes of compute and storage resources without any downtime for the database during resizing.
Automatic patching of the database engine and operating system by Microsoft with no action from the customer.
Any supported SQL Server version and edition, with full parity with the matching on-premises SQL Server.

services: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines

stem: What does the Hyperscale service tier of Azure SQL Database mainly provide?

choices.text: A full SQL Server instance with SQL Server Agent jobs, linked servers and cross-database queries for many databases.
Operating system access on the database host so that monitoring agents and other software can be installed there.
A shared pool of resources for many small databases whose usage peaks happen at different times of the day.
Very large databases with independently scalable compute and storage, plus fast backup and restore regardless of size.

stem: A company owns SQL Server licenses and is moving workloads to Azure SQL Database, Azure SQL Managed Instance and SQL Server on Azure VMs. It wants to use those licenses to lower costs. What should it use?

choices.text: Moving all databases into one elastic pool, which converts the existing licenses into shared pool resources.
The Azure Hybrid Benefit, which gives a discount on SQL Server licensing and is available for all three products.
The serverless compute tier, which removes the SQL Server license fee whenever the database is paused or idle.
Azure reserved VM instances, which discount VM compute in return for a one-year or three-year commitment.

services: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines

stem: Before migrating several on-premises SQL Server databases, a company wants to find out which features they use that Azure SQL Database or SQL Managed Instance might not support. What should it do?

choices.text: Create an elastic pool and move the databases into it, because the pool rejects any database with unsupported features.
Run an Azure SQL assessment with Azure Migrate or SQL Server enabled by Azure Arc to evaluate the instances.
Enable auto-pause in the serverless tier, because a paused database reports features it could not load at startup.
Register the on-premises servers with the SQL IaaS Agent extension, which converts unsupported features automatically.

stem: A company runs a LAMP-stack web application (Linux, Apache, MySQL, PHP) on premises. It wants a managed Azure service for the database with automatic backups and patching, and no change to the database engine. Which service should it use?

choices.text: Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server, because PostgreSQL accepts MySQL dump files without changes.
SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines, running SQL Server on Linux so that the stack stays on a Linux server.
Azure SQL Database, after converting the schema and queries from MySQL to Transact-SQL for the SQL Server engine.
Azure Database for MySQL flexible server, a fully managed service based on the MySQL Community Edition engine.

stem: A logistics firm's on-premises PostgreSQL database uses PL/pgSQL stored procedures, custom data types and geometric data. It wants a managed Azure service and minimal application refactoring. Which service should it choose?

choices.text: Azure SQL Managed Instance, because it provides near-100% compatibility with on-premises database engines.
Azure Database for MySQL flexible server, because it supports stored procedures and custom server parameters.
Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server, because it runs the community version of the PostgreSQL engine.
Azure SQL Database Hyperscale, because it scales storage independently for large geometric and custom data.

stem: Which TWO capabilities describe PostgreSQL, the engine behind Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Defining custom data types and adding extensions, code modules that queries can run inside the database.
Storing schemaless JSON items that are partitioned automatically across regions for global distribution.
Grouping related columns into column families queried by a SQL-like language of its own, such as CQL.
Keeping all data only in memory as key-value pairs for caching, so it is lost when the server restarts.
Storing and working with geometric data such as lines, circles and polygons in relational tables.

stem: A team uses Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server for a development database that is needed only during working hours. It wants to cut costs at night and on weekends without deleting the server. What should it do?

choices.text: Stop the server when it is not needed, because compute billing stops immediately while the server is stopped.
Move the database into an elastic pool, which bills only for the hours when queries run against the server.
Enable auto-pause in the serverless compute tier, which pauses the server after a configured idle delay.
Set the backup retention to the minimum, because the compute charge is calculated from the backup storage size.

stem: A developer is building a first prototype on Azure Database for MySQL flexible server. The database will see light, irregular use and must cost as little as possible. Which compute tier should she choose?

choices.text: The Memory-Optimized tier, because it gives the most memory per vCore for each connection the app opens.
The General Purpose tier, because it is the only tier that supports automatic backups and point-in-time restore.
The Burstable tier, which is designed for low-cost development and low-concurrency workloads like this one.
The Hyperscale tier, because it separates compute from storage and bills compute only while queries run.

stem: A company runs an important production database on Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server. It must stay available if an entire availability zone in the region fails, with no loss of committed data. What should it configure?

choices.text: The Burstable compute tier, which moves the server between zones automatically when it detects a failure.
Read replicas in the same zone, which take over writes automatically whenever the primary server stops responding.
A longer backup retention period, which lets the server restore itself in a new zone without losing any data.
Zone-redundant high availability, which keeps a warm standby in another zone with synchronous replication.

stem: Which TWO statements about Azure Database for MySQL flexible server are correct? (Select TWO)

choices.text: It gives administrators sign-in access to the underlying Linux VM to install their own tools.
It takes automatic backups and supports point-in-time restore for up to 35 days of retention.
It can be added to an Azure SQL Database elastic pool to share compute with other databases.
It is based on the MySQL Enterprise Edition and requires customers to bring their own licenses.
It is based on the MySQL Community Edition and is offered as a fully managed PaaS service.

stem: An online shop uses Azure Database for MySQL flexible server. Patches sometimes require a server restart, and the shop wants these to happen only at its quietest time, early Sunday morning. What should it configure?

choices.text: Manual patching through a remote session to the server, so that the shop installs each update by itself.
A custom maintenance schedule, so that automated patching is applied in the window that the shop chooses.
A read replica in another region, so that patches are applied to the replica instead of the primary server.
The stop and start feature, so that the server skips all patches while it is stopped on Sunday mornings.

stem: A DBA connects pgAdmin to Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server. Querying and monitoring work, but she cannot perform a server backup and restore the way she did on the on-premises server. Why?

choices.text: pgAdmin cannot connect to Azure Database for PostgreSQL, so the session is actually running against a local copy.
Backups require the Memory Optimized compute tier, and the server was created in the General Purpose tier.
The server is managed by Microsoft, so some server-focused functions such as server backup and restore are not offered.
The database must first be moved to an Azure SQL Database elastic pool before backup functions become available.

stem: A company is choosing between Azure SQL Database and SQL Server on Azure VMs for a new reporting database. Which statement correctly compares how they keep the SQL Server version current?

choices.text: Azure SQL Database always runs the latest stable engine and is updated by Microsoft; on a VM you choose and install the version and its updates.
Both services let you pick any SQL Server version, but only the VM option applies updates automatically without the customer's action.
SQL Server on a VM always runs the latest engine, while Azure SQL Database stays on the version chosen when the database was created.
Both services are updated by Microsoft on a fixed schedule, and neither allows the customer to choose an older SQL Server version.

services: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines
